catalog_quote: Stress is typically on the penultimate syllable, regardless of the number of syllables in the root, as could be seen in (2)–(4) above. Examples of roots with stress on the last syllable are e.g. aˈbi ‘sour’, maŋˈgo ‘banana’, bibiˈtoŋ ‘butterfly’ and amˈgor ‘shout’. See also minˈlen ‘woman’, pinˈca ‘side’ and taraˈmus ‘fairytale’, introduced in (2) and (3). Some of the words with root-final stress appear to be loans from Kalamang. This neighbouring Papuan language has unpredictable stress but has a slight preference for the right edge (Visser, 2022, 74). Examples are taˈpar ‘k.o. kangaroo’ and saˈnoŋ ‘thatched roof’, which have the same meaning and stress pattern in Kalamang. There are also words that are the same in Uruangnirin and Kalamang except for the stress: lusi ‘eagle’ is an example. In Uruangnirin, it is pronounced ˈlusi, in Kalamang luˈsi. [...] [§4] Similarly to other Austronesian languages, stress occurs typically on the penultimate syllable in Uruangnirin, although there is a fair number of examples with stress on the final syllable as well (section 2.5).
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root whatever its length (ˈsi.ka, ku.ˈte.na, ma.ka.ˈni.ni, ka.na.ˈba.raf); a lexically listed minority of roots carry final stress (aˈbi, maŋˈgo, bibiˈtoŋ, amˈgor, minˈlen, pinˈca, taraˈmus, kaˈsuk), several of them loans from Kalamang (taˈpar, saˈnoŋ), and the authors attribute the final-stress set to Kalamang contact. No weight conditioning is proposed; no antepenultimate or other patterns reported.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any of the three sources.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stress roots: aˈbi 'sour', maŋˈgo 'banana', bibiˈtoŋ 'butterfly', amˈgor 'shout', minˈlen 'woman', pinˈca 'side', taraˈmus 'fairytale', kaˈsuk 'man' (Visser 2026), taˈpar 'k.o. kangaroo', saˈnoŋ 'thatched roof' (Kalamang loans with Kalamang stress); contrast ˈlusi 'eagle' (Uruangnirin) vs luˈsi (Kalamang). Visser 2026 OTC p. 20 calls the final-stress exceptions 'many'. Visser 2026 sketch notes final-stressed minlen/kasuk reduplicate their final syllable (minlenlen, kasuksuk).
new_statements.domain_note: Stated over roots/citation forms ('regardless of the number of syllables in the root'); transcriptions are of isolated lexemes from a recorded wordlist (IPA with stress marks in the 1,400-item appendix). Nothing explicit on whether subject-index prefixes or reduplication shift stress; prefixes are pre-root so penult-of-root and penult-of-word coincide for suffixless forms. Phrase-level prosody deferred to Gunnarsson 2025 (phonological word / accentual phrase / intonational phrase).
new_statements.identity_note: All three Visser sources describe the Faur-Kiaba dialect (fieldwork in Kiaba village, 2022-2025); Visser 2026 OTC notes minimal dialect differences vs Tarak-Tuberwasak (lexical items, /ŋg/ > /g/ simplification), nothing said about dialectal stress differences. Language also called Rwangnirin / Wangnirin / Karas Darat. Glottolog urua1244 has no dialect subdivisions.

new_statements.quote: The distribution of the accent is consistent in Uruangnirin. Stress is lexically determined and typically falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable of a morphological word, though the great majority of words have penultimate stress (Visser 2024:8). In monosyllabic words, the only syllable is the place of accent. There is at least one minimal pair in the dataset where stress location is the only difference (asuˈban ‘to fish with rod’ and aˈsuban ‘to curse someone’). Since finally accented words are rare it is not weird that this is the only minimal pair in the dataset. The phonological word exhibits culminativity, with a single syllable being the most prominent [p. 9] ... Uruangnirin is a head-prominence language with lexical stress accent. [pp. 23-24]

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog penult rule and with Visser & Stickl 2025 sec. 2.5 (penult default, listed final-stress roots). Adds: stress is lexical/contrastive (minimal pair), realised as an H*L pitch accent, and only the last phonological word of an accentual phrase carries a fully realised accent; classifies Uruangnirin as a head-prominence, lexical-stress-accent language. The placement statement is second-hand (cites Visser 2024:8);diva-portal.org, then TCP timeout at 119 s), so the on-disk Internet Archive copy of was read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is a lexical property of the morphological word; it falls on the penultimate syllable in the great majority of words, on the final syllable in a minority (lexically listed, contrastive: asuˈban vs aˈsuban); each phonological word has exactly one stressable syllable (culminativity). Stress is realised as a bitonal H*L pitch accent (p. 20) which is fully realised only on the last phonological word of the accentual phrase (postlexical head marking, pp. 9, 23-24); the thesis also notes amplitude and duration cues but did not measure them.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; the thesis states each phonological word has a single stressable syllable and one accent, no mention of secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stress words (rare, lexically determined); minimal pair asuˈban 'to fish with rod' vs aˈsuban 'to curse someone'. The stress statement itself is credited to Visser (2024:8), an unreleased sketch-grammar manuscript, not to the thesis's own instrumental data; the thesis's own contribution is the intonational analysis (H*L accent on the AP-final word).
new_statements.identity_note: Gunnarsson's data are recordings from the ELAR Uruangnirin corpus (Visser et al. 2023) of the Karas-island speakers; no dialect distinction is drawn. The sketch's lexeme recordings (work 1) are by two speakers, Nur Ain Kanabaraf (b. 1977) and Badarudin Kanabaraf (b. 1982), per Visser & Stickl 2025 appendix note p. xxxvii.

sources.note: Sec. 2 'Phonology' p. clviii: 'Stress is typically on the penult (ˈfodan 'tikal leaf'), with some exceptions where stress is on the last syllable (kaˈsuk 'man'). Some of the words with final stress are loans from Kalamang (saˈnoŋ 'thatched roof').' Cites Gunnarsson 2025 for intonation (phonological word, accentual phrase, intonational phrase). Sec. on reduplication (p. clxii area): final-stressed minlen, kasuk reduplicate the LAST syllable (minlenlen, kasuksuk), attributed to their final stress.
